title: Feel the slope, take a stride
allegory: SGD is like walking down a hillside in thick fog: you cannot see the valley, so you feel which way the ground rises under your boots and take one stride the other way, again and again.
map: where you stand on the hill
the slope felt under your boots, pointing uphill
the gradient ∇L(θ); you step against it
loose scree making each reading a little off
the minibatch gradient: a noisy estimate of the full one
credit: Hillside picture borrowed from Andrew Ng's Machine Learning course (baby steps downhill); 3Blue1Brown's Neural Networks ch.2 uses the same ball-rolling-downhill framing.

chapters.name: Lost in fog
chapters.note: somewhere down there is a good model

cap.1: Training is a walk in thick fog. Somewhere below is the valley floor, where the model's mistakes are smallest, and you cannot see it.
cap.2: The loss is your altitude and the weights are your position. You never see the whole landscape; you can only measure the loss and its slope where you stand.
cap.3: The loss surface over millions of parameters is never seen globally. Each step has only local information: L(θ) and ∇L(θ) at the current θ, estimated on one minibatch.

cap.1: So you feel the ground under your boots, find which way is uphill, and take one stride the other way. Then you feel again. That is the whole method.
cap.2: The gradient points uphill, so you step against it; the learning rate is your stride. Each reading comes from a random batch of data, so it is a little off: that is the 'stochastic'.
cap.3: SGD: θ ← θ − η·ĝ, where ĝ is the minibatch gradient, an unbiased but noisy estimate of ∇L. Each step is cheap; η sets how far each local reading is trusted.

cap.1: Where you stand next = where you stand now, minus stride times slope. Minus, because the slope points uphill and you want to go down.
cap.2: p -= lr * p.grad for every parameter, inside torch.no_grad() so the update itself is not tracked for backprop. That line is the heart of the exercise.
cap.3: θ ← θ − η∇L(θ), applied in place under no_grad or inference_mode. Momentum, weight decay, RMSprop and Adam each modify the gradient or the step size; the skeleton stays.

cap.1: Distance from the valley floor, step by step. Short strides crawl, a good stride slides straight in, and a long stride bounces from wall to wall.
cap.2: On a simple bowl, every step multiplies your distance from the bottom by the same number, 1 − η·a. Small η: close to 1, slow. Too big: negative, so you land on the far side.
cap.3: For L = ½aθ², θₖ = (1 − ηa)ᵏθ₀: monotone for η < 1/a, oscillating for 1/a < η < 2/a, divergent beyond 2/a. Curvature, not the loss value, sets the safe step.

chapters.name: The forgotten reset

right.title: forgot zero_grad()
lines: steps grow, loss wobbles or explodes

chapters.verdict: PyTorch adds new gradients to old ones. Reset every step.

cap.1: A classic slip: forgetting to clear the last slope reading. Now every slope ever felt gets added up, so strides grow longer and point the wrong way.
cap.2: PyTorch accumulates .grad across backward calls. Skip optimizer.zero_grad() and each step uses the sum of all past gradients. No error; training just goes strange.
cap.3: Without zeroing, the step is η·Σₜ gₜ: momentum with μ = 1 and no damping, so it overshoots and oscillates. Accumulation is deliberate only for gradient accumulation over micro-batches.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Momentum, RMSprop, Adam: SGD plus one tweak
Learning rate: the first knob to sweep
Fine-tuning and RLHF run this same step

cap.1: Every fancier optimiser is this step with one tweak. Master the plain version and the rest are small changes.
cap.2: Momentum averages past slopes, RMSprop scales each parameter's stride, Adam does both, and AdamW adds clean weight decay. The learning rate is always the first knob to sweep.
cap.3: Fine-tuning, RLHF and SAE training all move weights this way, so knowing what one step does is the base layer for understanding, and steering, how training changes a model.

coda.title: Pick a stride for a bowl-shaped valley

curves.label: distance from the bottom after x steps

readouts.label: largest safe stride for this bowl, 2/a
verdict
readouts.f: abs(1 - lr*a) < 1 ? (1 - lr*a < 0 ? 'zigzags in' : 'slides in') : 'blows up'

caption.1: Drag the stride. Small: you crawl. Medium: you slide straight in. Too big: you bounce across the valley, and past a point you fly out of it.
caption.2: Each step multiplies your distance from the bottom by (1 − η·a). Below 2/a you converge; above it you diverge. Now make the bowl steeper and watch the safe stride shrink.
caption.3: For L = ½aθ², θ ← (1 − ηa)θ converges iff 0 < η < 2/a. With many directions the steepest curvature sets the limit, one motivation for per-parameter scaling in RMSprop and Adam.

where_else: Every optimiser you will use (momentum, RMSprop, Adam, AdamW) is this step plus a correction
Fine-tuning, RLHF and SAE training all run the same loop: compute a loss, step against its gradient
Fitting any curve by nudging its knobs against the error, from a straight-line fit to a frontier model

hamming.what: The basic learning step: move every weight a little in the direction that lowers the loss, scaled by the learning rate.
hamming.when: On every training step of every network you train, either directly or inside a fancier optimiser like Adam.
hamming.why: The gradient only tells you which way is downhill right here, so small steps trust that local reading only as far as it stays true.

object.title: The foggy ravine
object.subtitle: A valley with one steep pair of walls and a gentle floor, and a bead that can only feel the slope where it sits.

cap.1: A round bowl. The bead feels the slope, steps downhill, and rolls straight to the bottom.
cap.2: Equal curvature in every direction: every step points at the minimum, so plain SGD is at its best.
cap.3: Isotropic quadratic: the gradient points at the minimum, and one η suits every direction.

cap.1: Now a narrow ravine. The bead zigzags between the steep walls, then crawls along the gentle floor.
cap.2: Steep walls, gentle floor: the step that suits the walls is too small for the floor. That zigzag is SGD's signature.
cap.3: Ill-conditioned: per-step factors 1 − ηλ differ by direction; the steep axis oscillates while the shallow axis converges slowly.

cap.1: Tiny strides: no zigzag, but after 60 steps the bead is still far from the bottom.
cap.2: Too small a learning rate is safe and slow. The floor direction barely moves.
cap.3: Small η gives 1 − ηλ near 1 on the shallow axis: stable but slow, since convergence is limited by the smallest curvature.

cap.1: Strides too long for the steep walls: every bounce is bigger than the last, and the bead flies out.
cap.2: Past the safe limit for the steepest direction, each step overshoots further. This is a loss that suddenly shoots to NaN.
cap.3: η > 2/λ_max makes |1 − ηλ_max| > 1 on the steep axis: divergence, however gentle the other directions are.

cap.1: From above, the zigzag is plain to see. Momentum and Adam, the next ideas, exist to smooth it out.
cap.2: Momentum averages the zigzag away; RMSprop and Adam give each direction its own stride.
cap.3: Momentum damps the oscillating component; RMSprop and Adam rescale per parameter, which acts on axis-aligned differences in gradient scale.

predict.q: The bowl gets twice as steep. What happens to the largest safe learning rate?
predict.why: Each step multiplies your distance by 1 − η·a, so you need η < 2/a. Twice as steep means half the stride.

predict.q: You forget optimizer.zero_grad(). What happens to each step?

options.t: It uses the sum of every past gradient, so steps grow
Nothing: PyTorch clears gradients by itself

predict.why: PyTorch adds each new gradient into .grad. Without a reset, old slopes keep pushing, like momentum with no friction.

object.where: Any valley that is much steeper one way than another: badly scaled input features, and the loss surface of nearly every deep network.
